title: Livestreaming as the antidote to AI
content:
Last week, hundreds of thousands of people tuned into a day long livestream where Brian from The Office sat in a glass cube doing expense reports manually. The livestream was organized by Ramp, a financial services startup that offers easy-to-use corporate cards, bill payment and accounting software. One thing they do is automate expense reports.

The livestream was not just popular because it starred a beloved Office character and a slew of other popular TikTok content creators including The Rizzler, but because the programming was highly engaging and fundamentally ephemeral. The day ended with an actual live wedding.

I spent all weekend and part of last week at Twitchcon in San Diego surrounded by livestreamers, and have been thinking a lot about the role of live content specifically lately. While much of the content creator industry was dominated by short form a few years ago, live streaming is becoming more and more dominant as a format.

As I wrote recently in The Hollywood Reporter, viewers watched more than 20 billion hours of live content on Twitch in 2024, the equivalent of 2 million years, and Twitch paid out more than $1 billion to streamers last year. “Right now, the biggest stars in the world are all streamers,” Zack Honarvar, founder of Good Story Studios, an entertainment studio that works with creators, told me.

“Social media is increasingly not social, short form, impersonal, endless scrolling,” said Dan Clancy, CEO of Twitch. “We see Twitch and live content as the antidote to that.” Young creators like iShowSpeed, 20, and Kai Cenat, 23, have had a breakout year by developing long form programmatic content and narrative streams. iShowSpeed embarked on a world tour, giving viewers an unfiltered look into countries like China from the perspective of a Gen Z creator. Kai Cenat, meanwhile, took over an entire university campus where he hosted Steamer University, an online reality show to find the next big influencer. (read my full THR piece here).

The Ramp livestream was a perfect example of a brand effectively leaning into this format. Ramp also sponsors TBPN, the live tech news show that has exploded in popularity over the past year and become the defacto CNBC for all of Silicon Valley.

Kendall Tucker, who leads creative experimentation at Ramp, said that she and others at Ramp have been tracking the rise of live content and its popularity in contrast with AI slop.

“It was right after Kai Cenad did his 30 day livestream, we were talking about authenticity in the age of AI and how do you do something that’s real,” she said. “In an Age of AI where you’re afraid to question if something’s real on the internet, wanted to do something physical, so that users walking by and people walking by would post it and say ‘I saw this.’”

Ramp contracted Rohan Kumar, an internet guru who previously worked for MrBeast and MSCHF to help flesh out the idea. The team then began recruiting creators who could improve during 15 minute segments, each of which had its own loose plot points. The result was a highly compelling livestream that dominated people’s feeds. “We heard from major CEOs that they had the livestream as their second screen up all day,” Tucker said. “This is AI video counter culture btw,” one fan tweeted.

I think livestreaming will only become more ascendent as a format, especially given the rise of clipping. Political consulting shops are now paying clipping firms thousands of dollars to seed clips of their preferred candidates or boost right wing influencers across the internet, while the clipping agencies themselves are raking in millions of dollars.

Live content can be toxic, and plenty of that toxic behavior was on display at this year’s Twitchcon (I’ll be making a video about this). But it’s also raw and unfiltered and feels real in a way that other content formats just don’t anymore. In a time when everything online feels increasingly synthetic, I think more and more people will seek out the unedited chaos of livestreams.
